documents.title: Statement of Claim
blocks: International Chamber of the Commercial Court of the Canton of Bern

**Zytglogge Praezisionsinstrumente AG**, Nydeggstalden 14, 3011 Bern, Switzerland (UID CHE-114.270.558 MWST), Claimant, represented by Dr. Lukas Herrmann, Attorney at Law, Moser Herrmann Attorneys at Law, Bundesgasse 10, 3011 Bern

**Marchmont Dynamics Ltd**, 22 Riverside Business Park, Nottingham NG2 1RT, United Kingdom (registered in England and Wales No. 08234719), Respondent, represented, upon information and belief, by Dr. Priska Wenger, Attorney at Law, Wenger Clerc Attorneys at Law, Loewenstrasse 29, 8001 Zuerich
concerning: restitution and damages arising from a Master Services Agreement for the implementation of an enterprise resource planning system
The Respondent be ordered to pay to the Claimant GBP 336,000.00, plus interest at 5% per annum from 12 January 2026.
The Respondent be ordered to pay to the Claimant GBP 158,500.00, plus interest at 5% per annum from the date of filing of this Statement of Claim.
It be declared that the Master Services Agreement dated 14 May 2024 between the Claimant and the Respondent was validly terminated by the Claimant with effect from 12 January 2026.
Costs and legal fees to be borne by the Respondent.

The Claimant, Zytglogge Praezisionsinstrumente AG, is a Swiss stock corporation with its registered office at Nydeggstalden 14, 3011 Bern, Switzerland, UID CHE-114.270.558 MWST, entered in the Commercial Register of the Canton of Bern. The Claimant manufactures precision measuring instruments for the watchmaking and medical-device industries and employs approximately 230 people in Bern.

The Respondent, Marchmont Dynamics Ltd, is a private limited company incorporated in England and Wales under company number 08234719, with its registered office at 22 Riverside Business Park, Nottingham NG2 1RT, United Kingdom. The Respondent provides enterprise resource planning ('ERP') software implementation and integration services to clients across Europe, including Switzerland.

This dispute concerns the implementation by the Respondent, under the internal project name 'Project Compass', of a new ERP system for the Claimant's manufacturing operations in Bern. The implementation failed at Go-Live in late November 2025, the Claimant terminated the Master Services Agreement between the parties for the Respondent's default, and the Claimant now seeks restitution of the milestone payments it made and damages for its resulting loss. The Respondent disputes that it was in default and, upon information and belief, intends to counterclaim for its own unpaid invoices.

The Commercial Court of the Canton of Bern has jurisdiction over this dispute pursuant to Article 6 paragraph 4 letter c of the Swiss Civil Procedure Code ('ZPO'). This dispute concerns the commercial activity of both parties within the meaning of Article 6 paragraph 4 letter c number 1 ZPO; the value in dispute, set out at Rz. 6 below, far exceeds the threshold of CHF 100,000 fixed by Article 6 paragraph 4 letter c number 2 ZPO; the parties expressly consented to the jurisdiction of this Court in Clause 21.2 of the Master Services Agreement (Exhibit C-1), satisfying Article 6 paragraph 4 letter c number 3 ZPO; and, at the time that agreement was concluded, the Respondent had its seat outside Switzerland, satisfying Article 6 paragraph 4 letter c number 4 ZPO.

Pursuant to Clause 21.3 of the Master Services Agreement (Exhibit C-1) and Article 129 paragraph 2 letter b ZPO, the parties agreed that these proceedings, being an international commercial dispute falling within Article 6 paragraph 4 letter c ZPO, be conducted in the English language. This Court has, since 1 January 2026, conducted proceedings in English on this basis in appropriate international commercial matters.

The value in dispute is GBP 494,500.00, being the sum of the amounts claimed under Prayers for Relief 1 and 2, which corresponds to approximately CHF 568'675 at the indicative exchange rate of GBP 1 = CHF 1.15 prevailing on the date of filing. This value is stated for procedural purposes only and does not limit the relief sought.

No prior conciliation proceedings have taken place. None are required: pursuant to Article 199 paragraph 3 ZPO, where a single cantonal instance has jurisdiction under Article 6 ZPO, as is the case here, the claiming party may file its action directly with the court.

In 2023 the Claimant resolved to replace its legacy, locally-hosted ERP system, which no longer supported its manufacturing and reporting requirements. Following a competitive tender process, the Claimant selected the Respondent as the implementation partner for the new system.

On 14 May 2024 the parties executed a Master Services Agreement together with an accompanying Statement of Work ('SOW') (Exhibit C-1). The Master Services Agreement is, by its Clause 21.1, governed by the substantive law of Switzerland, notwithstanding the Respondent's domicile in England.

The total price for the services under the Master Services Agreement is GBP 420,000.00, exclusive of any value added or equivalent turnover tax, payable in five milestone instalments as set out in Schedule 2 to the Master Services Agreement: Milestone 1 (contract signature), 15%, GBP 63,000.00; Milestone 2 (design phase sign-off), 20%, GBP 84,000.00; Milestone 3 (build phase completion), 25%, GBP 105,000.00; Milestone 4 (user acceptance testing completion), 20%, GBP 84,000.00; and Milestone 5 (Go-Live and final acceptance), 20%, GBP 84,000.00 (Exhibit C-1).

The implementation was planned in three phases: Phase 1 (Design), Phase 2 (Build), and Phase 3 (Testing and Cutover), with Go-Live targeted for late November 2025, as set out in the Project Plan annexed to the SOW (Exhibit C-1).
Milestone 1 fell due upon signature. The Respondent issued invoice INV-2024-0071 on 21 May 2024, which the Claimant paid on 4 June 2024.

The Design phase ran from June to October 2024. The Claimant approved the Functional Design Document on 24 October 2024, triggering Milestone 2. The Respondent issued invoice INV-2024-0128 on 28 October 2024, which the Claimant paid on 11 November 2024.

During the Build phase the parties agreed two Change Requests under the change-control procedure of Clause 9 of the Master Services Agreement: CR-04, adding three management-reporting dashboards to the Finance module at no additional cost, approved on 9 January 2025; and CR-07, adding a one-way interface to the Claimant's existing warehouse management system, at an additional cost of GBP 5,700.00 for six consultant-days, approved on 24 March 2025.
The Build phase was completed and signed off on 30 May 2025, triggering Milestone 3. The Respondent issued invoice INV-2025-0054 on 3 June 2025, which the Claimant paid on 17 June 2025.

At its meeting of 29 August 2025, the parties' Steering Committee recorded the data-migration workstream as 'Amber', pending the Claimant's delivery of a validated extract of its legacy master data by the Data Freeze Date of 15 September 2025 fixed in the Project Plan (Exhibit C-4).
The Claimant delivered the complete, validated legacy master data extract to the Respondent in accordance with the Data Freeze Date fixed in the Project Plan.

User acceptance testing ran from October to November 2025. The Claimant accepted the user acceptance testing results in writing on 14 November 2025, triggering Milestone 4. The Respondent issued invoice INV-2025-0109 on 18 November 2025, which the Claimant paid on 26 November 2025 (Exhibit C-5); the payment is confirmed, together with the three preceding milestone payments, in the bank confirmation issued by the Claimant's bank, Aareland Bank AG (Exhibit C-6).

At its meeting of 14 November 2025, the Steering Committee recorded Go-Live readiness as 'Amber', contingent upon the Respondent resolving two outstanding Severity-1 defects in the General Ledger module, logged as GL-14 and GL-22, before cutover (Exhibit C-4). Following discussion, the Steering Committee confirmed that Go-Live would proceed as planned on 28 November 2025, on the basis that the Respondent would close those two defects beforehand.

Cutover to the live system began on Friday, 28 November 2025, as planned. The critical system failure that is the subject of this action - the System began posting duplicate entries to the General Ledger, corrupting the opening trial balance and forcing a halt to all customer invoicing and payroll processing - occurred on 30 November 2025 (Exhibit C-12).

The Claimant's on-site system administrator, Mr. Broennimann, and other members of the Claimant's IT team spent the remainder of the Go-Live weekend attempting to contain the failure and to restore the General Ledger from the Respondent's own backup appliance, without success, as the backup itself proved to be corrupted (Exhibit C-12).

On 3 December 2025, the Claimant's Head of Operations, Ms. Zbinden, gave the Respondent formal written notice of the critical defects and, invoking Clause 17 of the Master Services Agreement and Articles 366 and 107 of the Swiss Code of Obligations ('CO'), set the Respondent a period of ten working days, expiring 17 December 2025, within which to remedy the defects, failing which the Claimant reserved the right to withdraw from the Master Services Agreement (Exhibit C-7).

The defects were not fully remedied within the period set, nor at any time before the Claimant's withdrawal described at Rz. 25 below. The General Ledger module remained unusable for closing purposes for the whole of this period.

On 8 December 2025, the Claimant's project office issued an internal status report recording the General Ledger module as 'Red', with 47 open defects, 11 of them Severity-1, and noting that invoicing and payroll processing remained suspended (Exhibit C-8).

On 20 December 2025, the Claimant's Chief Executive Officer, Dr. Fankhauser, and Ms. Zbinden exchanged an internal e-mail reviewing the options open to the Claimant, including termination of the Master Services Agreement (Exhibit C-10).

By letter of its counsel dated 12 January 2026, the Claimant declared its withdrawal from the Master Services Agreement pursuant to Articles 366 and 107 paragraph 2 CO, demanded restitution of the milestone payments made within thirty days, and reserved the right to claim further damages (Exhibit C-9).

Following termination, the Claimant engaged a replacement systems integrator to stabilise the Claimant's finance function and to complete the ERP implementation, incurring cost of approximately GBP 97,000.00, and incurred a further approximately GBP 61,500.00 in business-interruption losses, comprising temporary staff, overtime and lost efficiency, while its invoicing and payroll processes remained impaired.
The Respondent has not repaid any part of the GBP 336,000.00 paid by the Claimant under Milestones 1 to 4, nor compensated the Claimant for its loss.

The Respondent was selected following a competitive tender conducted in 2023, in which the Claimant evaluated three candidate systems integrators against functional fit, cost and delivery track record; the Claimant selected the Respondent in April 2024 on the basis of its stated specialism in manufacturing-sector ERP implementations and its proposed delivery timeline of eighteen months to Go-Live.

The implementation was staffed, on the Respondent's side, by a team of up to six consultants led throughout by Mr. Fox as lead consultant, and, on the Claimant's side, by Mr. Huegli as project manager reporting to Ms. Zbinden, with Mr. Broennimann providing infrastructure and system-administration support.

During user acceptance testing between October and November 2025, 63 defects were logged, of which 58 were resolved before the Claimant accepted the test results on 14 November 2025; the remaining five, including GL-14 and GL-22, were carried forward on the basis of the Respondent's assurance, recorded in the Steering Committee minutes of 14 November 2025 (Exhibit C-4), that they would be closed before cutover.

GL-14 concerned the incorrect rounding of postings denominated in a foreign currency; GL-22 concerned an intermittent failure of the month-end accrual routine. Neither defect, properly understood, was of the same character or severity as the duplicate-posting failure that in fact occurred at Go-Live, which arose from a different part of the System's batch-import logic, as confirmed by the Claimant's independent expert (Exhibit C-11).

Throughout December 2025 and January 2026, the Claimant's finance team, supported by Mr. Broennimann, undertook interim manual closing and payroll procedures to keep the business operating while the General Ledger module remained unusable.

The Respondent's project team changed twice during the Build phase: the original lead consultant left the Respondent's employment in January 2025 and was replaced, after a six-week handover, by Mr. Fox. The Claimant was not consulted on either change, although Clause 2.2 of the Master Services Agreement required the Services to be performed substantially in accordance with the agreed Project Plan.

The cutover plan annexed to the Statement of Work provided for a rollback to the legacy system within four hours if cutover failed verification. No rollback was attempted or offered by the Respondent once the duplicate-posting defect appeared; instead, the Respondent chose to attempt a forward fix on the live System, a decision the Claimant was not asked to approve.

The suspension of invoicing and payroll processing directly affected the Claimant's manufacturing operations: two supplier payment runs were delayed beyond their contractual due dates, and the December 2025 payroll run for the Claimant's approximately 230 employees had to be processed manually outside the System, at the cost particularised at Rz. 27 above.

Characterisation of the Agreement. The Master Services Agreement is predominantly a contract for work within the meaning of Article 363 et seq. CO: the Respondent undertook to deliver a defined result - a functioning, tested ERP system accepted by the Claimant - and not merely to apply best efforts. The object of a contract for work may be immaterial, as the Federal Supreme Court has confirmed in respect of an intangible surveying result (BGE 109 II 34). To the extent particular work packages, such as the configuration work performed under the Change Requests, are instead characterised as a mandate within the meaning of Article 394 CO, the same remedies in substance apply by reason of the Respondent's default under Articles 97 et seq. CO.

The Respondent's default. The Respondent failed to deliver a System free of critical, use-preventing defects by the agreed Go-Live date, and failed to cure the defects notified on 3 December 2025 within the ten-working-day period set by the Claimant's notice - a period that itself exceeded the minimum reasonable period required by Article 107 paragraph 1 CO. Withdrawal from a contract for work under Article 366 CO as a rule presupposes that the customer has granted the contractor a period to cure under Article 107 CO, as the Federal Supreme Court held in BGE 98 II 113; that requirement was satisfied here.

Validity of the withdrawal. The Claimant was accordingly entitled to, and validly did, withdraw from the Master Services Agreement pursuant to Article 366 paragraph 1 and Article 107 paragraph 2 CO by the letter of 12 January 2026 (Exhibit C-9).

Restitution. Under Article 109 paragraph 1 CO, a party that withdraws from a contract may refuse the promised consideration and reclaim what it has rendered. The Claimant is accordingly entitled to restitution of the GBP 336,000.00 paid under Milestones 1 to 4, as confirmed in Exhibit C-6.

The Claimant anticipates that the Respondent may seek to invoke its own asserted delay in supplying the legacy master data extract as an excuse under Article 2 of the Swiss Civil Code. That defence cannot succeed: Clause 14.2 of the Master Services Agreement allocates the risk of data-related delay to the Respondent save to the extent it actually caused a resulting defect, and the critical failure here was a duplicate-posting error in the Respondent's own cutover script, unrelated to any data-quality issue, as confirmed by the Claimant's independent expert (Exhibit C-11).

Damages. Under Article 109 paragraph 2 CO, the Claimant is further entitled to damages for the loss flowing from the collapse of the Master Services Agreement, the Respondent having failed to show that its default was free of any fault. Where, as here, the contractor fails to remedy a notified defect, the customer may forgo the remedy and claim the cost of having the defect cured by a third party, applying Article 107 paragraph 2 CO (BGE 136 III 273). That cost, together with the Claimant's business-interruption loss, is set out at Rz. 27 above and totals GBP 158,500.00.

The Claimant's loss of GBP 158,500.00 comprises: (i) GBP 97,000.00 paid to its replacement systems integrator, itself comprising GBP 22,000.00 for emergency discovery and stabilisation of the General Ledger module and GBP 75,000.00 for completion of the outstanding elements of the Statement of Work; and (ii) GBP 61,500.00 in business-interruption loss, comprising GBP 28,000.00 for temporary finance staff, GBP 11,500.00 in overtime, and GBP 22,000.00 in lost efficiency during the period the General Ledger module remained unusable.

Limitation of liability. Clause 20.1 of the Master Services Agreement, to the extent it purports to exclude the Respondent's liability for grossly negligent conduct - here, proceeding to Go-Live on a finance module with known, unresolved Severity-1 defects - is void under Article 100 paragraph 1 CO and does not limit the Claimant's damages claim.

Article 377 CO does not assist the Respondent. Article 377 CO confirms the customer's unconditional right to terminate a contract for work for convenience before completion, against indemnification of the contractor (BGE 117 II 273); it has no application where, as here, the customer instead terminates for the contractor's default.

Interest. The Claimant claims interest at 5% per annum, the statutory default rate under Article 104 paragraph 1 CO, on the restitution claim from 12 January 2026, the date of the declaration of withdrawal, and on the damages claim from the date of filing of this Statement of Claim.

The Claimant bears, and discharges, the burden of proving the Respondent's default and the resulting loss under Article 8 of the Swiss Civil Code; the Respondent, conversely, bears the burden of proving any circumstance said to excuse that default, including the asserted contributory effect of the data-delivery timeline addressed at Rz. 41 above.

To the extent the Respondent seeks to set off its own disputed invoice against the Claimant's restitution claim, no set-off is available under Article 120 of the Swiss Code of Obligations: the Respondent's claim for Milestone 5 and the CR-07 charge did not fall due before the Claimant's valid withdrawal extinguished the Respondent's right to further payment under the Master Services Agreement.

Alternative legal characterisation. Should the Court conclude that particular elements of the Services, such as the work performed under CR-04 or CR-07, are better characterised as a mandate within the meaning of Article 394 CO rather than as part of the contract for work, the Claimant's termination remains effective and without liability to the Respondent: a customer terminating a mandate under Article 404 paragraph 1 CO owes compensation under Article 404 paragraph 2 CO only where termination occurs at an inopportune time, and termination following an uncured, use-preventing defect in the delivered System is not inopportune within the meaning of that provision.

Currency. The sums claimed are expressed and should be awarded in pounds sterling, being the currency in which the Master Services Agreement fixed the price of the Services and in which all milestone invoices, including Exhibit C-5, were issued and paid.

The Claimant requests that this matter be set down for a first case-management hearing at the Court's earliest convenience, given the ongoing accrual of interest and the Claimant's continuing reliance on manual workarounds for its invoicing and payroll functions pending final resolution of this dispute.

The Claimant requests that costs, including the court fee and the Claimant's reasonably incurred legal fees, be awarded against the Respondent in full, there being no basis on the facts pleaded above for any apportionment of costs.

Settlement discussions. Following the letter of 26 January 2026 (Exhibit R-7), the parties' counsel exchanged without-prejudice correspondence between February and April 2026 exploring a negotiated resolution, including a proposal by the Claimant to accept a reduced restitution sum in exchange for an accelerated payment timetable. No agreement was reached, and the Claimant does not rely on the content of those discussions in support of the relief sought in this Statement of Claim, which is advanced solely on the basis of the facts and legal arguments pleaded above.

Reservation. The Claimant reserves the right to adduce further evidence, including supplementary expert evidence on quantum and on the technical cause of the incident, and to amend or supplement this Statement of Claim, in response to the Statement of Defence and Counterclaim and in the course of these proceedings.

Exhibit C-1 Master Services Agreement and Statement of Work dated 14 May 2024. Exhibit C-2 Marchmont Dynamics Ltd Standard Terms and Conditions (excerpt). Exhibit C-3 Order Confirmation dated 16 May 2024. Exhibit C-4 Steering Committee minutes of 29 August and 14 November 2025. Exhibit C-5 Invoice INV-2025-0109 (Milestone 4). Exhibit C-6 Payment confirmation, Aareland Bank AG. Exhibit C-7 E-mail correspondence of 3 December 2025 (notice to cure). Exhibit C-8 Project status report of 8 December 2025. Exhibit C-9 Notice of withdrawal dated 12 January 2026. Exhibit C-10 Internal e-mail of 20 December 2025 (German). Exhibit C-11 Independent technical report of Dr. Elena Marti, Bantiger IT Forensics AG. Exhibit C-12 Incident log of Mr. Broennimann (handwritten, 29-30 November 2025).

documents.title: Statement of Defence and Counterclaim
blocks: International Chamber of the Commercial Court of the Canton of Bern

**Marchmont Dynamics Ltd**, 22 Riverside Business Park, Nottingham NG2 1RT, United Kingdom, Respondent and Counterclaimant, represented by Dr. Priska Wenger, Attorney at Law, Wenger Clerc Attorneys at Law, Loewenstrasse 29, 8001 Zuerich

**Zytglogge Praezisionsinstrumente AG**, Nydeggstalden 14, 3011 Bern, Switzerland, Claimant and Defendant to the Counterclaim, represented by Dr. Lukas Herrmann, Attorney at Law, Moser Herrmann Attorneys at Law, Bundesgasse 10, 3011 Bern
The claim be dismissed in its entirety.
The Claimant, as Defendant to the Counterclaim, be ordered to pay to the Respondent GBP 92,100.00, plus interest at 5% per annum from 5 January 2026.
Costs and legal fees to be borne by the Claimant.

The Respondent does not contest the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 6 paragraph 4 letter c ZPO, the use of the English language under Article 129 paragraph 2 letter b ZPO, or the absence of prior conciliation, as pleaded at Rz. 4 to 7 of the Statement of Claim.
The counterclaim raised in Part V below requires no separate conciliation, being exempt under Article 198 letter g ZPO as a counterclaim joined to pending proceedings.

The value in dispute on the counterclaim is GBP 92,100.00, corresponding to approximately CHF 105'915 at the indicative exchange rate pleaded by the Claimant, and is comfortably within the jurisdiction already established for the main claim.
II. Response to the Statement of Claim
Rz. 1 and Rz. 2 of the Statement of Claim, concerning the identity and status of the parties, are admitted.

Rz. 3 of the Statement of Claim is admitted as to the fact of the implementation, its failure at Go-Live and the Claimant's purported termination, but the characterisation of the dispute as one of straightforward contractor default is disputed for the reasons set out in Part IV below.
Rz. 8 and Rz. 9 of the Statement of Claim, concerning the tender process and the execution of the Master Services Agreement and Statement of Work on 14 May 2024, are admitted.
Rz. 10 and Rz. 11 of the Statement of Claim, concerning the contract price, the milestone payment schedule and the project phasing, are admitted.
Rz. 12, Rz. 13 and Rz. 15 of the Statement of Claim, concerning the invoicing and payment of Milestones 1 to 3, are admitted.

Rz. 14 of the Statement of Claim is admitted as to the existence, scope and approval dates of CR-04 and CR-07. It is denied that these were immaterial changes; their cumulative effect on the Respondent's delivery team during an already compressed Build phase is addressed at Rz. 24 below.
Rz. 16 of the Statement of Claim is admitted.

Rz. 17 of the Statement of Claim is denied. The validated legacy master data extract was in fact delivered only on 6 October 2025, three weeks after the Data Freeze Date of 15 September 2025, as shown by the e-mail correspondence between the Respondent's Mr. Fox and the Claimant's Mr. Huegli, in which the Claimant's own project manager acknowledges the delay (Exhibit R-2).
Rz. 18 of the Statement of Claim is admitted.
Rz. 19 of the Statement of Claim is admitted.

Rz. 20 of the Statement of Claim is admitted in part and denied in part. It is admitted that a defect affecting General Ledger postings occurred over the Go-Live weekend. It is denied that this occurred on 30 November 2025: the Respondent's own contemporaneous project-channel records, consistent with the Claimant's own internal incident log, show that the defect first appeared on 29 November 2025 at 23:40 (Exhibit R-6).
Rz. 21 of the Statement of Claim is admitted.

Rz. 22 of the Statement of Claim is admitted, save that, in the Respondent's view, the period set was unreasonably short given the complexity of the defect and the condition of the data supplied by the Claimant.

Rz. 23 of the Statement of Claim is denied. The Respondent identified the cause of the defect within approximately fifteen minutes of its first appearance and had a tested patch ready for deployment by the evening of 30 November 2025 (Exhibit R-6), and continued remediation of the historic ledger data into January 2026. In any event, as recorded in the minutes of the emergency Steering Committee call of 28 November 2025 (Exhibit R-10), the Claimant's own Head of Operations had herself confirmed that Go-Live could proceed as planned, which is inconsistent with the Claimant's present characterisation of the defect as attributable to the Respondent alone.
Rz. 24 of the Statement of Claim is noted; the Respondent has no knowledge of the Claimant's internal reporting and does not admit its contents.
Rz. 25 of the Statement of Claim is noted; its content is not known to the Respondent.
Rz. 26 of the Statement of Claim is admitted as to the fact of the purported withdrawal, but denied as to its validity, for the reasons set out in Part IV below (Exhibit R-7).

Rz. 27 of the Statement of Claim is not known to the Respondent and is on that basis denied. Without prejudice to that denial, the sums claimed are in any event disputed as to causation, reasonableness and quantum.

Rz. 28 of the Statement of Claim is denied. The Respondent's invoice INV-2025-0138 of 5 December 2025 remains outstanding (Exhibit R-3), and the Claimant's purported withdrawal is, for the reasons below, without legal effect.
III. Respondent's Own Statement of Facts

The Respondent was selected following a competitive tender in 2023 in which it proposed an eighteen-month delivery timeline to Go-Live, premised on the Claimant supplying conforming legacy data by the Data Freeze Date fixed in the Statement of Work and on the scope of the Services remaining stable through the Build phase.

From early in the Build phase, the Claimant repeatedly expanded the scope of the Services by way of Change Requests, including CR-04 and CR-07, which, although each was assessed at the time as having no impact on the Go-Live date taken in isolation, materially increased the cumulative burden on the Respondent's team during an already compressed Build phase and contributed to schedule pressure ahead of Go-Live (Exhibit R-1).

The Claimant's delay in supplying the legacy master data extract - received only on 6 October 2025, three weeks after the Data Freeze Date - further compressed the time available for data-quality testing ahead of Go-Live (Exhibit R-2).

On-premise hardware required for the Services, including the backup appliance later affected by the incident, was delivered to the Claimant's premises on 14 October 2024 and received without reservation (Exhibit R-5).

Cutover began as planned on 28 November 2025. At an emergency Steering Committee call convened that evening, the Claimant's Head of Operations confirmed that Go-Live should proceed notwithstanding the items then still open (Exhibit R-10).

The Respondent's lead consultant, Mr. Fox, identified the cause of the duplicate-posting defect within approximately fifteen minutes of its first appearance, escalated immediately to the Respondent's on-call team, and had a tested patch ready for deployment by the evening of 30 November 2025 (Exhibit R-6). Remediation of the historic ledger data continued into January 2026, in cooperation with the Claimant's own IT staff.

The Respondent issued invoice INV-2025-0138 on 5 December 2025 for Milestone 5 and the CR-07 charge, in the total amount of GBP 89,700.00, which remains unpaid (Exhibit R-3; see also the supporting timesheet, Exhibit R-9).

By letter of 20 January 2026, the Respondent reminded the Claimant of the outstanding invoice (Exhibit R-4). By letter of 26 January 2026, the Respondent's counsel rejected the purported withdrawal as unjustified and reserved the Respondent's rights (Exhibit R-7).

An independent technical assessment commissioned by the Respondent attributes materially greater weight to data-quality issues in the Claimant's legacy data than the report relied upon by the Claimant, and concludes that the additional testing time lost to the Claimant's own delay in supplying that data was a significant contributing cause of the incident, which cannot properly be separated from the absence of an idempotency safeguard identified by the Claimant's own expert (Exhibit R-8).
The Respondent has at all times acted in good faith to remedy the incident and has incurred significant uncompensated cost in doing so, including the consultant time recorded in Exhibit R-9.

In the eighteen months preceding the Go-Live weekend, the parties' relationship was cooperative and without material dispute: the Claimant paid Milestones 1 to 4 without objection or deduction, and raised no formal complaint about the Respondent's performance before the notice of 3 December 2025.

Beyond CR-04 and CR-07, the Claimant raised a further three informal scope changes during the Build phase that were absorbed without a formal Change Request, at the Respondent's own cost, in the interest of maintaining the project schedule: an additional reporting field for the Finance module, a revised chart-of-accounts mapping, and an extra round of user-interface changes to the Inventory module.

The Respondent's clause 18 professional indemnity insurance referred to in the Master Services Agreement is not engaged by this dispute, there being no third-party claim against the Claimant to which it could respond; it is accordingly irrelevant to the quantification of either party's claim.

Between 29 November 2025 and 15 January 2026, the Respondent's consultants, principally Mr. Fox, spent in excess of 140 hours on incident response and remediation beyond the hours recorded in Exhibit R-9, for which the Respondent has not invoiced and does not seek payment in these proceedings, save to the extent relevant to the indemnification claim at Rz. 42 below.

To the extent the Services are properly characterised as a contract for work within the meaning of Article 363 et seq. CO, the Claimant's own default - its delay in supplying usable legacy master data by the Data Freeze Date fixed in Clause 14 of the Master Services Agreement - excuses any corresponding delay or defect on the Respondent's part. A customer may not invoke a default to which its own breach materially contributed, and may not in good faith rely on Article 366 CO where it has itself failed to cooperate as required (Article 2 of the Swiss Civil Code).

The Claimant's own Steering Committee confirmed, at the emergency call of 28 November 2025, that Go-Live should proceed notwithstanding the then-outstanding items (Exhibit R-10). Having itself endorsed proceeding to Go-Live, the Claimant cannot in good faith now treat the consequences of that joint decision as a default exclusively attributable to the Respondent.

In the further alternative, significant elements of the Services, in particular the configuration and advisory work performed under the Change Requests, are mandate-like services within the meaning of Article 394 paragraph 2 CO, terminable at any time by either party. Even if the Agreement as a whole is characterised as a contract for work, the Claimant's termination on 12 January 2026 - after the Respondent had identified the cause of the defect within minutes, deployed a tested patch by 30 November 2025 and continued remediating the historic ledger data into January 2026 - was not a response to an unremedied default but a unilateral termination for convenience within the meaning of Article 377 CO, which confirms the customer's unconditional right to terminate before completion against indemnification of the contractor (BGE 117 II 273). The Respondent is accordingly entitled to full indemnification for the value of the work rendered and the profit it would have earned on completion of the Statement of Work.

Indemnification under Article 377 CO extends to the Respondent's positive interest in performance, that is, the profit the Respondent would have earned had the Statement of Work been completed, net of the cost it was thereby spared. On a conservative estimate, the Respondent's lost margin on the uncompleted balance of the Statement of Work exceeds the sum presently claimed by way of counterclaim; the Respondent reserves the right to quantify and claim that further amount in these or separate proceedings.

In the further alternative, if the Claimant's termination is treated as a revocation of a mandate under Article 404 paragraph 1 CO, it occurred at an inopportune time within the meaning of Article 404 paragraph 2 CO, namely while the Respondent was actively remediating the incident, and the Claimant is accordingly liable for the Respondent's resulting damage on the same basis.

In any event, and without prejudice to the foregoing, the quantum pleaded by the Claimant at Rz. 27 and Rz. 43 of the Statement of Claim is disputed. The Claimant has itemised cost and business-interruption components, but has not evidenced the scope of work undertaken by its replacement integrator against the outstanding elements of the original Statement of Work, nor the basis for the staffing and overtime assumptions underlying its claimed business-interruption loss, and the Respondent puts the Claimant to proof of both components.
The Respondent accordingly denies that it is liable in restitution or in damages and maintains that Milestone 5 and the CR-07 charge remain due and payable in full.

Under Article 8 of the Swiss Civil Code, the Claimant bears the burden of proving the Respondent's default, causation and the amount of its loss. The Respondent puts the Claimant to proof on each element, including the causal link between the alleged default and the items of loss pleaded at Rz. 27 and Rz. 43 of the Statement of Claim.

In the further alternative, and without prejudice to Part V below, should the Court find any part of the Claimant's restitution claim well-founded, the Respondent invokes set-off under Article 120 of the Swiss Code of Obligations against its own claim for invoice INV-2025-0138 and the indemnification claim pleaded at Rz. 42 above.

documents.title: Independent technical assessment
blocks: INDEPENDENT TECHNICAL ASSESSMENT - PROJECT COMPASS GENERAL LEDGER INCIDENT

I, Dr. Elena Marti, born 3 March 1975, residing at Scheibenstrasse 12, 3014 Bern, was instructed by Zytglogge Praezisionsinstrumente AG to assess the technical cause of the General Ledger incident of 29-30 November 2025. I hold a doctorate in computer science and have worked in forensic IT assessment for financial and manufacturing systems for over fifteen years. I confirm that I have no financial or personal interest in the outcome of this dispute, that I have not previously been engaged by either party, and that this report reflects my independent professional opinion.

I have reviewed: the Master Services Agreement and Statement of Work dated 14 May 2024; the Steering Committee minutes of 29 August and 14 November 2025; the General Ledger application and database logs for the period 28 to 30 November 2025, extracted from the Claimant's production environment; the backup appliance's diagnostic and snapshot logs; the incident log kept contemporaneously by Mr. Broennimann; and the Teams channel export for the Go-Live weekend.

The System's cutover process migrates journal batches from a staging database into the General Ledger using a batch-import routine. A correctly designed batch-import routine should be idempotent, meaning that re-running the same batch, whether deliberately or as a result of a retry after a transient failure, should not create duplicate postings. Idempotency is ordinarily achieved by recording a unique key for each imported batch and rejecting any batch carrying a key already recorded as processed.

The system logs show that duplicate postings to the General Ledger first appeared at approximately 23:40 on 29 November 2025. The logs record a transient network timeout during the import of journal batch JB-0417 at 23:38, followed by an automatic retry at 23:39 that resubmitted the same batch. No idempotency key check rejected the resubmission, and the batch was posted a second time, corrupting the opening trial balance. The backup appliance's most recent snapshot, dated 28 November 2025, was separately found to be corrupted at the file-system level and could not be used to restore the ledger; this appears to be an unrelated, pre-existing fault in the appliance's scheduled snapshot job.

The compressed data-quality testing window following the delayed delivery of the legacy master data extract reduced the time available to validate migrated journal batches before cutover, and I have considered whether this contributed to the incident. Having reviewed the content of batch JB-0417, I do not find that its substantive data was itself defective; the duplicate posting resulted from the batch being submitted twice, not from an error within the batch. In my assessment, the principal and proximate cause of the incident was accordingly the absence of an idempotency safeguard in the batch-import routine, which is a design and testing responsibility of the implementing contractor rather than of the client.

The incident was, in my opinion, primarily attributable to a defect in the cutover software - the absence of an idempotency safeguard against batch resubmission - rather than to the condition of the data supplied by the Client.

documents.title: Technical note
blocks: TECHNICAL NOTE - PROJECT COMPASS GENERAL LEDGER INCIDENT

I, Ian Castellan, was instructed by Marchmont Dynamics Ltd to review the technical cause of the General Ledger incident of 29-30 November 2025, including the report of Dr. Elena Marti of Bantiger IT Forensics AG dated 25 February 2026.

I agree with Dr. Marti that the proximate trigger of the duplicate postings was the replay of a migrated journal batch without an idempotency safeguard. I disagree, however, with the weight her report gives to that single factor. The migrated batch in question originated from the legacy data extract delivered by the Client only on 6 October 2025, some three weeks after the contractual Data Freeze Date, which left materially less time for data-quality testing than the Statement of Work envisaged.

I note that Marchmont's lead consultant, Fox, identified the cause of the defect within approximately fifteen minutes of its first appearance and had a tested patch deployed within roughly twenty hours, which in my professional experience is a materially faster response than is typical for a defect of this severity.

In my opinion, the delay in supplying usable legacy data was a significant contributing cause of the incident, alongside the absence of an idempotency safeguard, and the two causes cannot properly be separated when assessing responsibility.

documents.text:
# Note on the characterisation of IT implementation contracts under Swiss law

*This note is a synthetic exercise document prepared for the CourtOS test-fixture dossier `be-software`. It does not reproduce any actual publication, textbook or article, and any resemblance to a real commentary or author is coincidental and unintended. It is included in this dossier only to populate a realistic literature folder for the exercise.*

## 1. The characterisation question

A contract for the implementation of enterprise software, such as an ERP system, does not fit neatly into either of the two classical service categories of the Swiss Code of Obligations. Where the contractor promises a defined, testable result - a system that passes agreed acceptance criteria - the agreement is naturally characterised as a contract for work within the meaning of Article 363 et seq. CO, notwithstanding that the 'work' produced is intangible. Where, instead, the contractor's obligation is better described as the careful exercise of professional skill without a guaranteed result - for example, advisory or configuration support billed on a time basis - the mandate rules of Article 394 et seq. CO are the more natural fit.

## 2. Mixed agreements

In practice, a single master services agreement for an ERP implementation commonly combines both elements: a fixed-price, milestone-based core scope (pointing towards a contract for work) together with time-and-materials change requests or advisory support (pointing towards a mandate). Swiss doctrine generally resolves this by characterising each severable obligation according to its own content, rather than forcing the entire agreement into a single box, while recognising that the parties' remedies for a failure affecting the delivery of the system as a whole will usually be governed by the contract-for-work regime where that is the dominant characterisation of the agreement.

## 3. Practical consequence for remedies

The characterisation matters most at the point of termination. Under the contract-for-work regime, a customer facing an uncured, use-preventing defect may withdraw under Article 366 CO in conjunction with Article 107 CO, provided a reasonable period to cure has first been granted. Under the mandate regime, either party may terminate at any time under Article 404 CO, subject only to a damages claim where termination occurs at an inopportune moment. The two regimes can produce materially different outcomes on the same facts, which is why the initial characterisation of the agreement - and of any severable work package within it - is so often contested in practice.
